title: R' Chadqa
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: A tanna of baraitot, famous for his halakhic ruling in Shabbat 117b that a person is obligated to eat four meals on Shabbat; in the Yerushalmi, Shabbat ch. 16, halakhah 3, he is called R' Hindekes. He is also mentioned in a halakhic context in Sanhedrin 56b, where he adds that the descendants of Noah were also commanded to refrain from castration. In aggadah he is mentioned in Taanit 11b, where he said: a person's soul testifies against him; and in Derekh Eretz Zuta ch. 1 he said: 'Love “perhaps” and hate “what does it matter?”' (that is, not to say, 'What does it matter?'); and in Megillat Taanit ch. 12 he says: on the day that enemies sought to kill the sages of Israel, the sea rose and destroyed [supplied והשחתי; print and named scholion והשחית] a third of the inhabited world; and in Yalkut on Song of Songs, on 'Lereach shemanekha', he says: from this you learn that the fragrance of the righteous is pleasant and noticeable among the wicked.

And Hyman considers it very likely that he was among the first students of R' Akiva (Bava Batra 119a). And in Sifrei, Beha'alotekha, R' Chadqa said: Shimon HaShikmoni was a colleague of mine, among the students of R' Akiva.

notes.text: The sea narrative prints והשחתי, an irregular first-person verb in this context. The proposed English signals the difficulty without altering the Hebrew.

The heading's abbreviated title remains R', as do the separate Hindekes and Sifrei Chadqa/Akiva occurrences; neither contextual expansion of the name Akiva nor a full title in another work licenses title transfer. The scholion reads R' Chidqa (חידקא), with an abbreviated title and והשחית, 'and destroyed'; the supplied article has Chadqa (חדקא) and והשחתי, a first-person form irregular in this context. The bracketed English follows the bounded contextual third-person comparison while explicitly retaining the supplied letters. This does not prove a misprint, printed-page reading, correction history or identity between source forms. The sea rises and a third of the inhabited world is destroyed in that comparison; no first-person action by Chadqa is newly admitted. The earlier failed complex-book requests Megillat Taanit12 and12:1/HTTP400/KeyError remain historical failures, not evidence of global absence or successful witness retrieval. The Derekh Eretz scalar explicitly has full Rabbi Chadqa locally and the saying 'Love perhaps and hate what does it matter?'; that full title is recorded here only, without moving to the heading or separate passages. Hyman's explanatory gloss 'not to say what does it matter' is restored in the English; the supplied unmatched closing parenthesis remains exact in Hebrew, with English punctuation editorially paired. The older Shema-prayer implication is not adopted, and scrupulous hesitation remains contextual interpretation of perhaps rather than extra primary wording. Four Shabbat meals, the Noahide prohibition also concerning castration, the soul's testimony, enemies seeking to kill Israel's sages, one third, and the fragrance of the righteous among the wicked all remain Hyman's supplied claims; the other cited Shabbat/Sanhedrin/Taanit/Yalkut/Sifrei and Bava Batra passages were not newly checked. Very likely and first students preserve the strength and early-cohort claim of Hyman's argument, not an admitted chronology. Every older English version, both original mixed notes and the current note remain exact; the original note-revision request is not applied. The consulted scan of Hyman I, p. 411, actually prints והשחית, “and destroyed,” beside the supplied transcription’s והשחתי. The English records that printed third person without changing the Hebrew or the earlier notes about the irregular supplied form. The whole consulted Warsaw-labelled Megillat Ta’anit Adar scholion also reads והשחית and names Chidqa, חידקא, beside Hyman’s Chadqa, חדקא. It does not make Chadqa the first-person destroyer. Derekh Eretz Zuta gives “Love perhaps and hate what does it matter?”; Hyman’s own explanatory gloss is retained without turning “perhaps” into the Shema prayer. The whole Shabbat 117b passage gives Chidqa’s four meals beside the Sages’ three, and Sanhedrin 56b adds castration to the Noahide prohibitions. Bava Batra 119a explicitly reports Chidqa’s statement that Shimon HaShikmoni was his colleague among Rabbi Akiva’s students. This supports the reported saying, without independently proving Hyman’s stronger early-cohort reconstruction: “very likely” and “among the first students” remain his argument. The exact Sifrei parallel and other uncollated editions remain attributed; Chadqa, Chidqa and Hindekes are not globally merged. Extra scriptural proofs, legal opinions and narrative continuations are not inserted into the supplied biography.
